paragraphs.heading: What a feather is
paragraphs.text: A feather is a growth from the epidermis, the outer layer of skin, and together a bird's feathers make up its plumage. Birds have them, and so did some non-bird dinosaurs and other archosaurs. Of all the structures that grow from vertebrate skin, feathers are the most complex. Among living animals they help set birds apart from every other group. The study of feathers has its own name, plumology.

paragraphs.heading: What feathers do
paragraphs.text: Feathers help a bird fly, keep it warm and keep water off. Their colours help birds signal to each other and stay safe. Colour patterns can hide a bird from predators, and they can also hide predatory birds as they look for a meal. Feathers may also be plucked to line a nest, keeping eggs and young warm.

paragraphs.heading: Shaft, barbs and hooks
paragraphs.text: There are two basic kinds of feather: vaned feathers on the outside of the body and down feathers underneath. Vaned feathers, also called contour feathers, grow from set tracts on the skin and cover the whole body. Each has a central shaft, the rachis, with side branches called barbs. The barbs branch again into barbules, and these carry tiny hooks, the barbicels, that latch onto their neighbours. At its base the rachis widens into a hollow tube, the calamus or quill, which sits in a follicle in the skin.

paragraphs.heading: Why down is so warm
paragraphs.text: Down feathers have no barbicels, so their barbules hang loose instead of hooking together. That loose tangle holds air, which makes down an excellent insulator. Goose and eider down have great loft: squeezed flat, they spring back and trap lots of insulating air in small pockets. Because feathers are soft and hold heat so well, they fill pillows, blankets and mattresses, as well as winter coats and sleeping bags.

paragraphs.heading: Built from keratin
paragraphs.text: Feathers form in tiny follicles in the outer skin that make keratin proteins. The kind in feathers, called β-keratin, is made of protein strands bonded into pleated sheets, then twisted and linked together. The result is tougher than the α-keratin in mammal hair, horns and hooves. Flight feathers are stiff enough to push against the air on the downstroke but give way in other directions. In birds that fly, the keratin fibres line up along the shaft toward the tip more neatly than in flightless birds.

paragraphs.heading: Heavier than the bones
paragraphs.text: A single feather is light, yet a bird's whole plumage weighs two or three times as much as its skeleton. That is because many bird bones are hollow and hold air sacs. For flying, the most important feathers are the remiges on the wings and the rectrices on the tail.

paragraphs.heading: Feathers and people
paragraphs.text: Large bird feathers, most often from geese, have been used to make quill pens, and the word pen comes from the Latin penna, meaning feather. In French, plume can mean a feather, a quill or a pen. Hunting wild birds for ornamental feathers once put some species in danger and helped drive others to extinction. Feathers for fashion and military dress now come as a by-product of poultry farming and are dyed and worked to improve their look.
